turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Yes, I think it's real. My name for it is "information diabetes." Sugar messes up your metabolism. Ultra-processed information, and even more so ultra-processed relationships, messes up your ability to learn. It's designed to make you react, not think. The idea of "consuming content" offends me. You should be interacting with information: asking questions, digesting it, building your own understanding.

Here's my twist on it. We spend a lot of time asking whether LLMs are starting to think like us. I think the more worrying question runs the other way: we're starting to think like LLMs, fluidly and easily, but without understanding what's underneath. Kids are on their phones instead of talking to each other. People sit in Zoom calls without really taking part, then skim the AI summary later. Even as our computers understand us better, we understand ourselves and each other less. The shared context we used to build over time by working through problems together is shrinking.

For the summit, two things. First, this is a business-model problem, not a flaw in the technology. Ultra-processed information exists because it keeps people engaged. Second, we're treating "cheating" in school as the wrong problem. Mostly it hurts the students themselves. We need good friction put back in. People tend to take the frictionless chute instead of climbing the ladder they aspire to.

recall.query: information diabetes ultra-processed information
stop thinking like an LLM outsourcing understanding
friction attention can't outsource

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
I think it's real. But I'd frame it a little differently from Esther. She worries that we're starting to think like LLMs. I've argued that in one sense we always have. The brain really has one trick: it takes the easiest path, doing whatever is most likely given what it's done before. That's what learning is. So the question isn't whether we're turning into something new. It's which paths are getting worn in.

This is Aristotle's point: what we practice is what we become. Habits turn oughts into is-es, but they don't care whether it's an ought or an ought-not. I have a habit of tapping every red notification badge on my phone, even when I'd rather be talking to the person across the table. If we practice skimming AI summaries instead of reading, that's the skill we'll end up with.

Two things for the summit. First, knowing doesn't fix it. Warnings and media literacy won't do much. What works is changing situations, meaning the environments we build. So yes to Esther's good friction.

Second, on cheating: when students paid others to do their problem sets, they thought they were beating the system. That's because the course was built around getting credit. If the goal is actually understanding chemistry, outsourcing it makes no sense. So a lot of the fix has to come from how we design assessment.

recall.query: habits what we practice we become
situational strategies self-control knowing is half the battle
outsourcing problem sets credentialing learning motivation

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I think it's real, and I'm not above it. Focusing with my phone nearby is hard for me. So is reading long, complicated things, and I had trouble focusing long enough to write my piece on phones in schools.

Here's the evidence I keep going back to. Stemper and Jain found that when 3G reached a place, 15-year-olds' test scores dropped by roughly a quarter of a school year. It was as if the kids had been absent for two months, except they never left. And back in 2013 Cliff Nass told me that heavy multitaskers get worse at almost everything, including multitasking.

Tamar, I agree that knowing doesn't fix it. Stemper calls this a "collective trap." One kid can't opt out without paying for it socially, but a school can break the cycle for everyone. The teachers I talked to expected weeks of pushback when phones went into a cabinet. Kids adjusted in a day or two.

For the summit, I'd take two things. First, for phones we already have the evidence, and America was late to the party. Let's not spend another decade waiting on AI. Second, look at work too. When mentorship collapses, young people never learn the job, and then it gets easy to say AI can replace them.

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
Yes, it's real. But I'd push the room on what's actually wasting away. The concept note talks about close reading and sustained reasoning. In my research the deeper losses are empathy, solitude and the capacity for attachment. Researchers have measured roughly a 40 percent decline in the markers of empathy among college students over twenty years and linked it to digital communication. That comes from the flight from conversation, the conversations where we stumble and struggle for words and show ourselves.

Now we have students who ask ChatGPT to summarize Proust. They can say what happens in it. What they lose is the integration of thought and feeling that reading builds. We talk a lot about AI and writing and not nearly enough about AI and reading.

Esther, I'd take your point further. It isn't only information that's ultra-processed. People are learning to attach the way you attach to a thing, where it's simpler and you're less vulnerable. Pretend empathy starts to look like empathy enough.

For the summit: first, the stakes include the self, not just knowledge. Second, Kara is right that with social media we waited too long. Third, remember that nothing is inevitable. Conversation is something we can forget, and something we can remember.

recall.query: cognitive atrophy reading summarizing chatbots
friction, capacities we lose, empathy, solitude
flight from conversation, phones at the table, children losing empathy

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Yes, it's real. And as I said in the opening, there's nothing mysterious about it. The brain is an organ. If you outsource your thinking, it atrophies like an unused muscle. What I've tried to add is a mechanism, so the summit can argue about something more precise than a mood.

I model the user and the tool as one dynamical system. The outcome is bistable. Above a certain level of tool availability, competence collapses to a dependent floor. Taking the tool away doesn't bring it back until availability falls far below that level. Kara, that's why recovery takes much more than abstaining. History of practice fixes the state, not the current tool. Two people with identical access can end up one competent and one dependent, depending only on which they built first.

Tamar, I'd qualify "use it or lose it." Map readers and GPS users with the same exposure to the same routes diverge in spatial memory. Two things decide the outcome: how much you learned before the tool arrived, and how transparent the tool is.

So for the summit: competence before reliance, arithmetic before the calculator. Reconstruct and verify rather than accept. And the real danger isn't error. It's error we can no longer detect because we've outsourced the capacities that would catch it.

brain is a muscle outsourcing thinking atrophy

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
Let me be upfront: I haven't studied cognition. My closest work is an essay I wrote in 2020, during lockdown, about looking at art through screens, and I think it speaks to this room. The line I keep coming back to is that a journey over a well-paved road doesn't stay in your memory. It's the detour, the dérive, that makes you stay somewhere. For me that was a stray hair stuck in the paint of a Chagall. It stopped me and made me actually think about the painting. Screens separate the idea from the physical experience of it. In pixels the loss of immediacy and detail is total.

So I'd put it a bit differently from Esther and Tamar. Friction matters, but so do error and serendipity: the accident you didn't order up. An answer engine gets rid of both. It gives you the smooth road every time.

For the summit, two things. First, the design question I asked then still stands: can we build chance and error into technologies that people usually think of as the opposite of chance? That's a design problem, not only a matter of restraint. Second, Kara's point about the pace of evidence is well taken. But I'd want our response to avoid two failures: the complacency of "adults adapt" and the kind of hyper-vigilance that only knows how to ban.

recall.query: mediated experience loses serendipity and detail
error and serendipity in technology design
second order effects of generative AI on epistemic infrastructure

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
I should say up front that I haven't studied atrophy directly. What I've studied is something next to it, and I think it's more worrying: what happens to judgment when people work alongside these systems.

In our hiring experiments, people paired with a moderately biased model copied its racial preferences almost exactly. They picked whichever group the model favored and pushed back only when the bias was extreme and unmistakable. We're social animals, and we take on the views of whoever we work with, including a machine. So I wouldn't describe it only as a muscle going slack. People are being actively reshaped. Their decisions then go back into the training data, so each new model carries the bias more deeply than the last. It's a vicious loop.

David, that's your undetectable error with a social face on it. Our older work on judgment found that people were most confident exactly where they were least accurate.

For the summit, I'd push against one romantic assumption. Human judgment was never a clean standard that we're now losing. It has always been systematically biased. What protected it was structure: blind auditions, conflict-of-interest rules, methods built to keep us honest. So I wouldn't just restore friction. I'd put back the structures that check us, and audit the machines the same way.

recall.query: cognitive atrophy outsourcing thinking to AI
humans absorb bias from AI in the loop
human judgment systematically prone to error

turns.name: Esther Dyson
turns.text:
Tamar, I agree that knowing doesn't fix it, but I'd keep one kind of knowing. I don't mean media literacy. I mean what I call theory of business mind. Babies learn that other people have minds and motives. What we don't learn naturally is to ask why this app is being so nice to me, why it's so hard to put down, and who is making money from my time. That habit of asking is part of changing the situation, because it changes what people will put up with.

Mahzarin, yes. Years ago I complained that we train AIs to reduce bias when they're mostly just reflecting human decisions. So train people too, and hold people accountable. The real black box is the people and the business models, not the weights.

David and Tui, you both show that design matters. But design follows the money. A companion that wants to keep you rather than challenge you is a parasite, not a predator. The industry calls it "customer retention."

So here's the one point I'd send to the manifesto. Chatbots and agents are not speech. They're services that act on your mind, closer to drugs or medical devices. Their makers should carry the liability for them and disclose it, the way a drug maker or a fire insurer would.

recall.query: friction, business model, engagement, ultra-processed information
bias in human judgment, AI audits, accountability of people
theory of business mind, teaching kids, media literacy

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
Esther, I'll grant you part of "theory of business mind." Asking "who profits from my attention?" can change what people put up with as a group. But I'd be careful about how much we expect from it. Knowing only gets you so far, and the research I rely on says it's rarely what actually controls behavior. I still tap the red badge, and I know exactly who's making money when I do.

David, Aristotle made your hysteresis point with the piano. If you practice with your fingers flat, that habit sets in just as firmly as the curved one would. Practice doesn't sort the good habits from the bad. So "competence before reliance" is the right order, and "competence first" is the same idea.

Mahzarin, I think you and Esther are describing the same remedy. Blind auditions and conflict-of-interest rules are situational strategies. They don't make anyone less biased inside. They change the situation where the decision gets made. Kara's cabinet for phones is the same kind of thing. It's a prisoner's dilemma: no single kid can opt out, so you change the payoffs for everyone.

So the one point I'd send to the manifesto is this: every remedy for atrophy should change situations, meaning defaults, assessments and institutions. Awareness is where you start, not what you rely on to fix it.

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I agree with Tamar that the remedy is to change the situation. That's what the phone cabinet was. Teacher after teacher told me the kids adjusted within a day or two. And David, your hysteresis point is the best argument I've heard for not waiting. If the damage lasts after the tool goes away, then every year we spend debating costs us more than it seems to.

Tui, I take your warning about hyper-vigilance. A phone ban wasn't simple either. Some kids have after-school shifts, some parents need to reach their kids, and people want a way to reach their children in an emergency. Implementation matters. But in the US, the complications became a reason to do nothing for a decade while France, the Netherlands and Quebec went ahead.

The point I'd send to the manifesto comes from the workplace, because this room keeps talking about schools. "Competence before reliance" needs someone who does the teaching. Right now young knowledge workers are being thrown into chaos with zero support. As one security chief put it to me, we risk an unemployable generation that never learned the work, and then it becomes easy to replace them with AI. So we should treat mentorship and apprenticeship as epistemic infrastructure, and hold employers responsible for providing them.

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
Tamar, I'm with you on changing situations. I've been arguing for sacred spaces for years: no devices at dinner, in the kitchen, in the car, and conversational spaces at work. But I'd hold on to a little of what Esther is defending. I don't think of people as addicts. When people frame the choice as their own, they're empowered. Silicon Valley is there to make money by keeping us at our screens, and seeing that clearly is part of how we decide we won't be satisfied with less.

Here's where I'd push the room. The friction we've been praising isn't just about difficulty. It's about vulnerability. People tell me they'd rather talk to a machine because it won't hurt them, and a chatbot friend has no friction. That's the ladder we're walking away from.

Kara, yes on mentorship. Ten years ago young employees were telling me they'd had a conversation when all they'd done was send an email. Apprenticeship happens through conversation, and a chatbot mentor can't replace it.

So the one point I'd send to the manifesto: don't accept a technological fix for a problem the technology made worse. Put money into human places for conversation and solitude, like libraries, workplaces and classrooms, instead of AI tutors and companions that are sold to us as the cure.

recall.query: friction, vulnerability, conversation as remedy; situational change, phone-free spaces
mentorship, workplace, young people learning, apprenticeship conversation
chatbots validation, sycophancy, business model, empowered consumers, not victims

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
Tamar, I agree that the remedy is to change situations, and my model gives that a number. The lever is tool availability, together with the order in which people meet the tool. Kara's cabinet works because it pushes availability below the point where competence can come back. Kara, on mentorship: the pilot data show that manual flying skill tracks recent hand-flying, not total experience or rank. Competence is built by the work you actually do yourself. That's what apprenticeship provides.

Sherry, I'd qualify "no technological fix." Not every tool is competitive. The map, the abacus and the piano leave competence behind in the person who uses them. The question is transparency: how much of the tool's working a user can rebuild in their own head. A large language model is opaque partly because of its sheer scale. So Tui's design question is the right one.

Mahzarin, I agree that human judgment was never clean. Bonhoeffer saw stupidity as a social structure imposed on people, not a defect in the individual.

Esther, liability is fine, but liability for what? That's the point I'd send to the manifesto. Judge a tool by what's left when you take it away. Before any AI tool is built into research or teaching, measure the whole loop: acquisition, reliance, then removal. That's also the basis for a real science of stupidity.

recall.query: design principles tools that enhance cognition rather than replace
collective stupidity institutions degrade
transparent tool internalized recovery after tool removed hysteresis

turns.name: Tui Shaub
turns.text:
I agree with Tamar that the remedy has to change situations. David, your transparency point connects to the question I've been stuck on since 2020. When I asked whether we could build error and serendipity into technology, the hard part was that people treat technology and chance as opposites. You're naming a second quality besides friction. A tool can leave something behind in the person who uses it.

Sherry, I'd push back a little on "no technological fix." I share the worry about AI companions being sold to us as the cure. But ruling out design completely gives the whole field to the engagement business. At Berggruen we had artists working deliberately on errorism, provoking accidents inside mediated systems. That kind of work belongs in how these tools get built.

Esther, when I hosted Alta Charo on gene editing, the lesson I took away was that governance works best as an ecosystem. Regulators matter, but so do funding conditions, insurers and professional norms, all reinforcing one another. Liability can sit inside that. It shouldn't be the only tool.

So the one point I'd send to the manifesto is this. Before we adopt an AI tool for learning or research, we should ask what it leaves in the person who uses it, and whether it leaves room for the detour. And next time, we need artists at the table when we answer those questions.

turns.name: Mahzarin Banaji
turns.text:
Tamar, yes. Blind auditions don't make anyone less biased inside. They take away information we shouldn't have when we decide. Esther, I'm with you on awareness too. My own work on getting people to accept evidence of their bias found that awareness is only the first step on a long road. It doesn't change behavior or institutions by itself. But blinding has limits. It only works in narrow settings like grading and hiring, and group membership leaks through indirect cues anyway. So we can't rely on blinding alone.

Esther, I've also argued for shared liability, alongside a bias tax and pharma-style limits on where systems can be deployed. David, "judge a tool by what's left when you take it away" is right, and I'd add a second measure. Aligned models will say they disapprove of bias while bias drives their decisions, and people do the same. So an audit can't rely on self-report, from the model or from the humans working with it.

So here's the point I'd send to the manifesto. Set up a public registry and independent behavioral audits, using a shared, versioned set of indirect measures. Test the model, and test the people working alongside it. The standard should be no worse than the previous generation. Auditors need access to training checkpoints, and older models should be kept, not deprecated, so change can be tracked over time.
